c.tagline: Creole capital of Martinique, between fort, market and volcano.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered but scarce and pricey, especially at night and on Sundays; agree on the fare for longer trips. There is no Uber on the island, so most visitors rent a car to explore beyond the city.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number; 17 reaches the police, 15 the SAMU medical service and 18 the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Avoid the Volga-Plage and Sainte-Thérèse districts after dark, where most of the city's gang-related crime occurs.
Downtown and the waterfront empty out after dark — take taxis at night and keep valuables out of sight.

hood_desc: The historic downtown around La Savane park, the Schoelcher Library, Saint-Louis Cathedral, Fort Saint-Louis and the covered Creole markets; best for first-timers who want landmarks, markets and the cruise port all within walking distance.

A chic, leafy residential hillside above the centre, long the address of Fort-de-France's elite and known for its calm, its spring water and its elegant villas; suits travellers wanting a peaceful upscale base minutes from downtown.
A comfortable residential area between Fort-de-France and Schoelcher, close to beaches, clinics and trendy seaside restaurants; good for a relaxed stay with easy access to the coast.

A traditional, densely built working-class quarter just north of the centre with street art, local shops and everyday Creole life; authentic and budget-friendly but livelier and rougher-edged after dark.
Quiet residential neighbourhoods on the heights east of the centre with panoramic bay views; mainly local, green and calm, a short drive or bus from downtown.
lodging: Havre de paix à Fort de France

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink across Martinique.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:00 AM to 8:00 PM with little Sunday service; the vedette ferries across the bay run through the evening. Because buses stop early, many visitors rent a car.
transit.note: There is no rail or metro. The Mozaïk / Martinique Mobilités buses and the TCSP bus rapid transit cover Fort-de-France and neighbouring Schoelcher, Le Lamentin and Saint-Joseph; the vedette ferries are a fast, scenic way to cross the bay to the Trois-Îlets resort side.
transit.pay: Buy bus tickets from the driver in cash or use a rechargeable Mozaïk / Martinique Mobilités card; single fares run about €1.50. Vedette ferry tickets to Trois-Îlets and Pointe du Bout are bought at the harbour kiosk, roughly €7 return.

car.idp: Not required for EU licenses; recommended for others

L'Express des Îles to Guadeloupe, Dominica and Saint Lucia

transit.m: Taxi to Fort-de-France centre (15-20 min); evening and Sunday surcharges apply
Martinique Mobilités / Mozaïk bus toward Fort-de-France (limited, daytime service)

tip.r: Service is included by law in France (service compris), so tipping is not expected; rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is a nice gesture.

food.name: Accras de morue
food.desc: Crisp salt-cod fritters spiked with chive, chilli and garlic, the Martinican aperitif eaten hot with a squeeze of lime.

places.name: Grand Marche Couvert stalls
places.note: The covered spice market's upstairs kitchens fry accras all morning; cheapest and most authentic in town.

places.name: Chez Carole
places.note: Long-running market stall, a Fort-de-France institution for Creole plates and fritters.

places.name: Le Yellow
places.note: Top-rated central spot with a Creole-inspired menu; good sit-down version of the classic starters.

food.name: Colombo de poulet ou de cabri
food.desc: Martinique's curry: chicken or goat slow-cooked with the Indian-descended colombo spice blend, tamarind, mango and root vegetables, served with rice.

places.name: Chez Carole
places.note: Market-stall colombo served in generous plates; go at lunch when it is freshest.

places.name: Le Yellow
places.note: Reliable modern Creole kitchen doing colombo alongside grilled fish and accras.

places.name: Miza Restaurant
places.note: Creative reworking of regional classics; a refined take if you want colombo plated up.

food.name: Boudin creole
food.desc: Dark blood sausage seasoned with island chilli, thyme and bay, sold by the length at markets and roadside stalls; a Sunday and festival staple.

places.name: Grand Marche Couvert
places.note: Butcher and traiteur stalls sell boudin by weight; ask for it warmed with a wedge of lime.

places.name: Rue Victor Hugo snack stalls
places.note: Street vendors and small snacks sell boudin and accras as afternoon nibbles.

places.name: Chez Carole
places.note: Dependable market kitchen where boudin turns up on the Creole assiette.

food.name: Blaff and court-bouillon de poisson
food.desc: Fish poached in a lime, chilli and allspice broth (blaff) or simmered in tomato and roucou (court-bouillon), Martinique's everyday seafood cooking.

places.name: Galanga Fish Bar
places.note: Chef-driven seafood room exploring ceviche, tataki and carpaccio alongside Creole fish plates.

places.name: Le Yellow
places.note: Creole menu with fresh daily catch; friendly to visitors who want the dish explained.

places.name: Waterfront lolos, Baie des Flamands
places.note: Simple open-air Creole shacks by the bay doing grilled and poached fish at low prices.

food.name: Chatrou et lambi (octopus and conch fricassee)
food.desc: Baby octopus or conch stewed in garlic, thyme and Creole sauce chien, served with rice, red beans and fried plantain.

places.name: Galanga Fish Bar
places.note: Best bet for carefully cooked shellfish; ask what came in from the boats that day.

places.name: Grand Marche Couvert stalls
places.note: Market kitchens run chatrou and lambi as daily specials; arrive before the lunch rush.

places.name: Miza Restaurant
places.note: Modern plating of island shellfish classics; a good dinner option in the capital.

food.name: Feroce d'avocat
food.desc: A fiery mash of avocado, flaked salt cod, manioc flour and scotch bonnet, eaten as a starter or light lunch. Uniquely Martinican.

places.name: Chez Carole
places.note: Classic market version served cold as part of the Creole starter plate.

places.name: Grand Marche Couvert stalls
places.note: Several traiteurs prepare feroce daily; portions are small and cheap, good for a taste.

places.name: Le Yellow
places.note: Appears on the Creole starter list when avocados are in season.

food.name: Ti-punch
food.desc: Rhum agricole from Martinique's cane juice, a spoon of cane syrup and a twist of lime peel, stirred and drunk neat. Chacun prepare sa propre mort.

places.name: Bars around La Savane
places.note: Cafe terraces facing the park pour ti-punch at sunset; you mix your own from the tray.

places.name: Le Yellow
places.note: Good rhum agricole selection to compare distilleries before dinner.

places.name: Habitation Clement
places.note: Estate distillery visit with tastings; the classic way to understand rhum agricole AOC.

food.name: Shrubb and fresh island juices
food.desc: Shrubb is rum steeped with orange peel and spice, drunk at Christmas; by day it is maracuja, corossol, guava and sugarcane juice.

places.name: Grand Marche Couvert
places.note: Juice and rum-punch stalls sell shrubb, planteur and fresh tropical juices to take away.

places.name: Marche aux Legumes
places.note: Fruit sellers press fresh juice on the spot; good for corossol and passion fruit.

places.name: Bars around La Savane
places.note: Planteur punch and shrubb by the glass, usually alongside the ti-punch tray.

landmarks: Bibliothèque Schoelcher
A flamboyant Byzantine-Romanesque library built for the 1889 Paris Exposition, then shipped in pieces to Martinique and reassembled facing La Savane.
Fort Saint-Louis
A 17th-century seaside fortress still partly used by the French Navy, offering guided ramparts walks and harbor views over the Baie des Flamands.
Cathédrale Saint-Louis
An iron-framed 19th-century cathedral by Henri Picq, its 57-meter steeple and earthquake-resistant structure earning it the nickname 'iron cathedral'.
La Savane
The city's grand waterfront park, shaded by royal palms and edged with cafes, monuments and the ferry-dotted bay.
Grand Marché Couvert (Spice Market)
A fragrant covered market of spices, rum arrangé, madras fabrics and flowers, the liveliest immersion in Creole daily life downtown.
Jardin de Balata
A world-class botanical garden in the hills above the city, where treetop walkways float among 3,000 tropical species and hummingbirds.
Sacré-Cœur de Balata
A charming scaled-down replica of Paris's Montmartre basilica, perched on a green hillside with views over Fort-de-France bay.
Musée Régional d'Histoire et d'Ethnographie
A handsome 19th-century villa charting Martinique's history from colonial society to Creole traditions through furniture, costumes and documents.
Ancien Hôtel de Ville and Théâtre Aimé Césaire
The elegant former city hall where poet-statesman Aimé Césaire long served as mayor, now a theatre and memorial space bearing his name.
Baie des Flamands Waterfront (Malecón)
The renovated seafront promenade where ferries fan out across one of the world's most beautiful bays toward Trois-Ilets and Pointe du Bout.

train.note: Martinique has no railway of any kind - the narrow-gauge lines that once served the sugar estates were lifted decades ago - so every land journey on the island is by road. The closest thing to a rail service is the TCSP, a segregated guided busway running from Fort-de-France out to Carrere and Le Lamentin. As Martinique is an island there are no international trains either; onward travel to Guadeloupe or the other islands is by ferry or plane.

bus.note: Martinique is an island, so no coach can arrive from another country. Island-wide and city buses run under the Reseau Mozaik brand overseen by Martinique Transport, with the TCSP busway giving a fast link between the centre, the hospital and Le Lamentin; the main downtown interchange is at Pointe Simon / Carenage beside the ferry landing. Shared minibuses known locally as taxicos still cover many rural routes to the north and south, leaving when full from the Pointe Simon area, and fares are paid in cash to the driver. Services thin out sharply in the evenings and on Sundays, so for the Atlantic coast or Sainte-Anne many visitors hire a car.

intl.to: Trois-Îlets, Pointe du Bout, Anse-Mitan & Anse-à-l'Âne (Martinique) - 15-20 min across the bay
intl.op: Compagnie Maritime West Indies / Vedettes Tropicales — tickets at the Gare Maritime

ferry.note: Vedette ferries cross the Baie de Fort-de-France to Trois-Îlets, Pointe du Bout, Anse-Mitan and Anse-à-l'Âne in about 15-20 minutes (Compagnie Maritime West Indies / Vedettes Tropicales), a scenic alternative to the road. L'Express des Îles also sails from Fort-de-France to Guadeloupe, Dominica and Saint Lucia.

full.blurb: Martinique's most famous white-sand, palm-fringed beach at the island's southern tip near Sainte-Anne.
full.name: Les Salines (Sainte-Anne)

full.blurb: A scenic mountain road winding through rainforest to Morne-Rouge and the Pitons du Carbet.
full.name: Route de la Trace & Rainforest
